prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Colleagues have now ranked B031 first or near the top in six of eight ballots (three first places), and I think that reflects the evidence and not just the habit of a measurement-minded committee. The lattice clock rests on one concrete idea, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so the light shift cancels while Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed. That idea was realized experimentally and then pushed by orders of magnitude through careful systematic control, with uncertainties and stabilities at the 1e-18 level, comparisons between independent clocks, and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements. Many separate laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed each other, which is the kind of reproducibility I weigh most heavily. It has already enabled further work: relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, many-body spin-exchange physics in the lattice, and a concrete route to redefining the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a theory-and-first-demonstration pioneer (Katori) and the group that drove the accuracy frontier and the many-body regime (Ye), within the supplied names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005) for the frequency comb and Wineland (2012) for ion control and ion clocks cover adjacent ground, and a committee could read the lattice clock as a very well executed refinement of recognized work. There is also a real priority question that I cannot settle from memory: the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and others to the early Sr clocks and to the idea itself are not in the credited names. And the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the strongest applications are still prospective.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B031 first and calls it original and lastingly important with relatively uncontested credit, but worries it may be seen as incremental on optical frequency standards (2005) and ion clocks (2012), and that weighting Katori against Ye rests on memory.
responses.response: I share the worry about overlap, but I do not think it is decisive. The comb gave the clockwork for counting optical cycles and the ion clocks control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock solves a different problem, interrogating very many neutral atoms with negligible perturbation, which is what brought stability (not just accuracy) to the 1e-18 regime and opened the many-body clock physics. On the weighting, I see Katori as the origin of the magic-wavelength idea and of the first demonstrations and Ye as the one who delivered the extreme performance, so I would not rank one over the other. The citation I propose therefore names the invention and realization, not a ranking of the two.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs discovery (B005) first as the natural experimental completion of the 2013 prize and proposes the founders Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, while admitting that choosing three from thousands is contestable, and ranks B031 third as a clean two-person metrology prize.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is scientifically beyond dispute, and I put it sixth only because of the attribution problem, not the science. Where I disagree is on how to treat that problem. The founders-versus-spokespeople question you raise is exactly the kind that cannot be settled by evidence in the record: Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee all have defensible claims, and any three will be called arbitrary by a large part of the community. A prize that is solid on science and weak on attribution is at greater risk than one that is solid on both, which is why I would put B031 ahead. I would still like to hear from you whether the founders reading of ATLAS and CMS credit survives scrutiny of who actually decided the detector designs.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B009) first, as an instrument invention that broke a long-standing resolution limit and brought sub-angstrom imaging of atoms in materials, with clear three-person credit and fully mature impact.
responses.response: This is the candidate closest to my own measurement-first view, and I find the Rose, Haider, Urban split by theory, construction and demonstration persuasive. Where I qualify your ranking is the open question you yourself raise about Krivanek and the STEM corrector, which weakens the claim that the three supplied names capture the decisive credit, and the 'physics versus technique' question that a physics committee will have to answer. B031 faces the same question about metrology, but its scientific payoff (tests of fundamental physics and a redefinition of the second) is more direct. I would keep B009 as my first alternative if the committee wants an instrument-and-measurement prize in this cycle.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B024) first as a theory-then-experiment story that created moire quantum matter, reproduced by many groups, with the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity still debated.
responses.response: I find the field's impact impressive, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiments is a clean story. My reservation is the one you list yourself: sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder make quantitative comparison with theory hard even now, and the experimental first author (Cao) is not among the credited names. The field is also less than a decade old, and several colleagues (Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, who all place it sixth) consider it premature. I would not oppose it in a later year, but I think the evidence base for B031 is more settled today.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes when judging the distinctness of the lattice clock, and whether a citation can state this clearly.

The detailed priority and credit split between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstrations, including the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates, which I am recalling from memory and have not verified.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before honoring the work.
Whether a second concurrent achievement (for example B009) would strengthen the configuration or only dilute it, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B031 from my profile: I have no listed link to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups. For B016 (circuit QED) my WACQT leadership role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, and Goran Johansson's own flagged connection there means B016 should be discussed carefully, though I am not a direct collaborator of the credited names. My PhD stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder is a distant mentor-network tie to the 2005 prize area, and I disclose it for transparency, as it relates to the JILA tradition behind Ye's group, but I do not regard it as requiring recusal.
